{{Short description|Property of an arithmetical theory}}
{{Lowercase title}}
In [[mathematical logic]], an '''ω-complete theory''' is a [[Theory (mathematical logic)|formal theory]] in [[first-order logic]], containing arithmetic, such that whenever it proves every natural number instance of a formula, it also proves the corresponding universal sentence. A theory with the complementary property is called '''ω-incomplete'''. The ω in the name refers to the set of [[natural number]]s.

The terminology was established in the 1958 paper ''The Classical and the ω-Complete Arithmetic'' by [[Andrzej Grzegorczyk]], [[Andrzej Mostowski]], and [[Czesław Ryll-Nardzewski]].<ref name="GMRN">{{cite journal |last1=Grzegorczyk |first1=Andrzej |last2=Mostowski |first2=Andrzej |last3=Ryll-Nardzewski |first3=Czesław |year=1958 |title=The Classical and the ω-Complete Arithmetic |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=188–206 |doi=10.2307/2964398 |jstor=2964398}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Consider a first-order language that contains [[Term (logic)|terms]] for the natural numbers <math>\bar 0, \bar 1, \bar 2, \ldots</math>. For example, the standard language for [[Peano arithmetic]] contains the two symbols <math>0, S</math>, with which we can write down the terms for all the natural numbers: <math>0, S0, SS0, \dots</math>.

Let <math>T</math> be a theory in the language. <math>T</math> is '''ω-complete''' iff, for every formula <math>\varphi(x)</math> with one [[Free variables and bound variables|free variable]],<math display="block">
T \vdash \varphi(\bar n) \text{ for every } n \in \omega
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
T \vdash \forall x\,\varphi(x).
</math>The implication may appear obvious. However, one must distinguish between <math>\vdash</math>, which is a [[Logical consequence|consequence]] within the object-theory, and <math>\implies</math>, which is a consequence in the meta-theory. A theory is ω-complete if it can perform this consequence within the object-theory, rather than perform it outside in the meta-theory.

== Examples ==
It is possible for a theory to be ω-incomplete, because the theory may have a model <math>\mathcal M</math> with [[Non-standard model of arithmetic|non-standard integers]]. In the model, we can have <math>\mathcal M \models \varphi(\bar 0), \mathcal M \models \varphi(\bar 1), \dots</math>, but nevertheless have <math>\mathcal M \not\models \varphi(c)</math> for a certain non-standard integer <math>c</math> in the model.

A standard weak example is [[Robinson arithmetic]] <math>Q</math>. It proves each instance of <math>0+\bar n=\bar n</math>, while the universal sentence <math>\forall x(0+x=x)</math> lies beyond its theorems. This can be computably demonstrated by building a computable nonstandard model of <math>Q</math>, in which <math>0 + c \neq 0</math> for a non-standard integer element <math>c</math>. Accordingly, <math>Q</math> is ω-incomplete.<ref name="SmithDef">{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Peter |title=An introduction to Gödel's theorems |publisher=Logic Matters |isbn=979-8-6738-6213-1 |edition=2 |location=England|year=2013|url=https://www.logicmatters.net/resources/pdfs/godelbook/GodelBookLM.pdf}}</ref>

[[Peano arithmetic]] repairs many weak failures of that kind, yet standard incompleteness arguments still yield ω-incompleteness under the usual consistency assumption. In particular, Gödel's second incompleteness theorem provide an example. Consider a [[Gödel numbering]] of all proofs in PA, and let <math>\varphi(\bar n)</math> to mean "If number <math>n</math> is a valid proof in PA, then its conclusion is not <math>0 = 1</math>". Then, <math>PA\vdash \varphi(\bar 0), PA\vdash \varphi(\bar 1), \dots</math>, but <math>PA\not\vdash \forall x \varphi(x)</math> by incompleteness. This argument applies to any recursively axiomatized theory that contains PA.<ref name="SmithQ">{{cite book |last=Smith |first=Peter |title=Gödel Without (Too Many) Tears |url=https://www.logicmatters.net/resources/pdfs/GWT2edn.pdf |date=2022 |publisher=Logic Matters |isbn=978-1-9169063-5-8 |edition=2 |location=Cambridge |pages=90–93}}</ref>

== Relation to nearby notions ==
ω-completeness is closely related to [[ω-consistency]]. A theory is ω-consistent when no formula <math>\psi(x)</math> yields both the existential sentence <math>\exists x\,\psi(x)</math> and every numeral instance <math>\neg\psi(\bar n)</math>.<ref name="SmithDef" /> The two notions mark different syntactic patterns in the study of formal theories.

By the [[Gödel's completeness theorem|completeness theorem]], a consistent theory is ω-incomplete if and only if it can be extended to a consistent but ω-inconsistent theory.

ω-completeness is also connected with the [[ω-rule]],<math display="block">
A(0), A(1), A(2), \ldots \;\Rightarrow\; \forall n\,A(n).
</math>[[Proof calculus|Proof systems]] using the ω-rule build the passage from all numeral instances to the universal conclusion directly into the proof system.
